To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
manganese inhibits amylase secretion by displacing calcium from binding sites in the pancreatic cell membrane.
Mn2+ inhibits acetylcholine-stimulated amylase secretion by displacing Ca2+ from membrane binding sites, and that this effect is not due to a competitive interaction with extracellular Ca2+.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of manganese, calcium and cobalt on amylase release from the rat pancreas.

the effects of manganese, calcium, and other divalent cations on amylase release from the isolated perfused pancreas of the rat, and with the effects of the same cations on the uptake and efflux of calcium from the gland.
the effects of manganese on pancreatic secretion and calcium homeo-stasis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the inhibitory action of Mn2+ on amylase release from the isolated pancreata is due to the ability of Mn2+ to displace Ca2+ from membrane binding sites involved in the secretory mechanism and to a reduced ability of manganese to replace the Ca2+ in the secretory system.

Mn(2+), in a dose-dependent manner, stimulates amylase secretion from the pancreas by displacing membrane bound Ca(2+) which is required for the secretory mechanism, and that Mn(2+, in a dose-dependent, time-dependent manner, inhibits secretagogue-stimuated secretion by competing with the secretagogue for the binding site on the membrane and/or by displacing Ca(2+ from the membrane, thus reducing the Ca(2+) available to activate the secretory

Mn2+ inhibits the secretagogue-stimulating action by competing with Ca2+ at the binding site of secretagogue receptors and/or by competing with Ca 2+ at the secretory mechanism, and that Mn2+ also inhibits the secretory mechanism by competing with Ca+2 at the secretory Ca2+ channel.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Mn(2+), Co(2+) and Ca(2+) all act as secretagogues for pancreatic acini.
Mn(2+), Co(2+) and Ca(2+) all have a similar effect on amylase output and (45)Ca exchange, and that Mn(2+)/Co(2+) and Mn(2+)/Ca(2+) interactions occur at the cellular level.

Mn(2+), like Ca(2+)(10(-2)m), evokes amylase secretion by displacing Ca(2+) ions bound to the membrane, and the resulting increase in intracellular Ca(2) concentration activates the secretory mechanism, but Mn(2+) also has an inhibitory effect on the secretory process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Mn(2+), Co(2+), and Ca(2+) are all capable of stimulating amylase release, but only Mn(2+) can inhibit the effects of secretagogues.
Mn(2+), Co(2+) and Ca(2+) are able to stimulate amylase secretion from the isolated pancreata of young rats.
